section.title: The Grief of God
section.sectionRationale: The world that began so good has filled with corruption. A mysterious boundary is crossed, human wickedness reaches its full height, and God looks on a heart that is only evil all the time. This tight unit moves from the spread of sin to the sorrow of God and His resolve to judge, and ends on a single hinge of hope: Noah found favor.
section.thesis: When human wickedness reaches its full flood, God is grieved to the heart and resolves to judge, yet one man finds favor, and grace survives the coming storm.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the boundary crossed and the limit set; the grief of God and the sentence of judgment; and the one bright exception, Noah's favor.

units.label: The boundary crossed
units.note: corruption spreads, a limit is set

verses.text: Now when men began to multiply on the face of the earth and daughters were born to them,
the {{sonsofgod|sons of God}} saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose.
So the LORD said, “My Spirit will not contend with man forever, for he is mortal; his days shall be 120 years.”

The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and afterward as well, when the sons of God had relations with the daughters of men. And they bore them children who became the mighty men of old, men of renown.

units.label: The grief of God
units.note: the heart of man, the heart of God

verses.text: Then the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that every {{inclination|inclination}} of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time.
And the LORD {{regretted|regretted}} that He had made man on the earth, and He was {{grieved|grieved}} in His heart.
So the LORD said, “I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth, every man and beast and crawling creature and bird of the air, for I am grieved that I have made them.”
Noah, however, found {{favor|favor}} in the eyes of the LORD.

sonsofgod.gloss: Literally sons of God. The phrase is debated: it may mean rebellious angelic beings, the godly line of Seth intermarrying with the ungodly, or powerful royal, tyrant figures. Elsewhere it can name angelic beings, but here it names those whose sin helps fill the earth with corruption before the flood.

inclination.gloss: A shaping, framing, or inclination, from the verb to form. Every yetser of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil continually. The word describes the bent of the heart, its settled direction; the same term recurs in 8:21, where God notes the heart is evil from youth yet promises not to curse the ground again.

regretted.gloss: To be sorry, to relent, to be moved to compassion or grief. The LORD regretted that He had made man. This is the same root as the comfort hoped for in Noah's name; here it expresses God's deep sorrow over sin, not a change in His character or a mistake in His plan.

grieved.gloss: To be pained, hurt, grieved. God was grieved in His heart, the very word used for the pain of the fall in 3:16. Human sin is no light thing to God; it wounds Him. This is a startling window into a God who feels the offense of evil deeply.

favor.gloss: Grace, favor, unmerited kindness. This is the first time the word grace appears in the Bible. Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD; the account will show Noah as righteous, yet the order here puts grace first, foreshadowing the gospel pattern of grace that precedes and produces a changed life.

basic.context: The world God made good has gone badly wrong. People multiply, but so does evil. A strange line is crossed by the mysterious sons of God, and human wickedness grows until every thought of the heart is evil all the time. God looks at all this with sorrow. The question is whether anyone is left who pleases Him.
basic.hermeneutics: This really happened, and it explains why the flood is coming. The hard question is who the sons of God are, and readers have long disagreed. But the main point is clear: sin has filled the earth, it grieves God's heart, and He resolves to judge, yet one man, Noah, finds grace.
basic.originalLanguages: Every inclination, the yetser, the bent of the human heart, was only evil all the time. God regretted, nacham, making man and was grieved, atsab, in His heart, the same word as the pain of the fall. Yet the passage ends on grace, chen, the first time that word appears in the Bible, resting on Noah.
basic.typology: Noah, the one man who finds grace and through whom the world is spared, is a picture of Christ, the one righteous man through whom a new world is saved. The grief of God over sin points ahead to the cross, where God bears the full weight of that grief Himself.
basic.christ: Noah finding favor in the eyes of the LORD points to Jesus, the truly favored and righteous One through whom God rescues a people from judgment. And God's heartbreak over sin is answered at the cross, where the grief of God meets the judgment of God in the death of His Son.
basic.god: This is a tender and sobering picture of God. He is not cold about evil; it grieves Him to the heart. He is holy and just, resolving to judge a world gone wholly corrupt. Yet even in His sorrow, grace appears, and He fixes His eyes with favor on one man.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 24 says the days of Noah picture the coming of the Son of Man. 1 Peter 3 and 2 Peter 2 recall Noah and the flood. Ephesians 4 warns us not to grieve the Holy Spirit, echoing God grieved here.
basic.oneStory: Sin, loosed in the fall and spread through the generations, now floods the whole earth and grieves the heart of God. Judgment is coming. But the story does not end in sorrow: grace lands on one man, Noah, and through him God will carry His purposes and His promise safely toward Christ.

context.literary:
These eight verses close the toledot of Adam that began at Genesis 5:1, and the next heading, 'This is the account of Noah,' opens at 6:9. The passage is therefore an epilogue to the whole pre-flood world and a prologue to the flood. It is framed by a phrase: humanity multiplies 'on the face of the earth' in verse 1, and God resolves to blot humanity out 'from the face of the earth' in verse 7. What began as fruitfulness under blessing ends as a sentence of removal from the same ground.

Two panels stand side by side. Verses 1 to 4 are compressed and allusive, with the sons of God, the daughters of men, a word from the LORD, and the Nephilim. Verses 5 to 8 are clear and theological, with the LORD's seeing, His grief, His resolve and His favour. The first panel describes what happened on the earth; the second describes what happened in the heart of God.

The language deliberately replays earlier scenes. The sons of God 'saw' that the daughters of men were 'beautiful,' literally good, and 'took,' verse 2, the three verbs of Genesis 3:6, where the woman saw that the tree was good and took. The LORD 'saw' the wickedness of man, verse 5, a grim reversal of Genesis 1:31, where God looked on all He had made and it was very good. The verb 'multiply' in verse 1 comes from the same root as 'great' in verse 5: humanity grew, and so did its evil. The list in verse 7, man, beast, crawling creature and bird, runs through the creatures of Genesis 1 in reverse order, as though creation were being wound backward.

The unit turns on its final verse. The Hebrew begins with the name, 'But Noah,' and the whole of verses 5 to 7 hangs in the air until that word arrives. The name also answers Lamech's naming in Genesis 5:29. The son born for comfort is the man on whom favour rests, and his name and the word for favour are made of the same two consonants in reverse order.
context.historical:
The first hearers lived among peoples who told stories of gods mingling with humans. Greek and Near Eastern legends spoke of heroes born of divine fathers and human mothers, and the Mesopotamian hero Gilgamesh was said to be two parts god and one part man. The phrase 'the mighty men of old, men of renown,' verse 4, sounds like the language of such legends. Genesis does not celebrate them. It sets them inside a story of corruption that ends in judgment, as if to say that the famous heroes of the ancient world were part of the problem, not its glory.

The Mesopotamian flood stories are also in the background. In the Atrahasis epic the gods send the flood because the growing human population makes too much noise and disturbs their rest. Genesis gives a completely different reason. The problem is not human numbers or noise but human hearts, 'every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil,' verse 5, and the response is not irritation but grief. Israel's God judges because He is morally serious, and He grieves because He cares for what He has made.

For Israel the Nephilim were not merely a memory. The spies in Canaan reported, 'We even saw the Nephilim there,' Numbers 13:33, connecting the giants of the land with this ancient race. The note in verse 4 that the Nephilim were on the earth 'in those days, and afterward as well' may be the narrator's way of linking the two. A generation facing strong enemies in the land was being told that giants had appeared before, and that God had dealt with a whole world of them.

In later Judaism these verses were read at length. The Jewish book known as 1 Enoch, which Jude quotes, told how angels called Watchers came down, took human wives and fathered giants. That reading was widespread in the centuries around the time of Jesus, and it shapes the background of several New Testament texts on angels who sinned.
context.canonical:
The title 'sons of God' appears elsewhere in the Old Testament for heavenly beings. They present themselves before the LORD in Job 1:6 and 2:1, and they shout for joy at creation in Job 38:7. Deuteronomy 32:8 in the BSB, following the older witnesses, speaks of the peoples' boundaries set 'according to the number of the sons of God.' The Nephilim reappear only with the spies in Numbers 13:33.

The diagnosis of the human heart in verse 5 runs through Scripture. After the flood God says the same thing, 'every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth,' Genesis 8:21, but now as the reason for patience. Moses says of Israel, 'I know their inclination,' Deuteronomy 31:21. Jeremiah calls the heart 'deceitful above all things and beyond cure,' Jeremiah 17:9, Psalm 14:2-3 pictures the LORD looking down to see if any seek Him and finding none, and Paul gathers these texts in Romans 3:10-12. Jesus says that 'out of the heart come evil thoughts,' Matthew 15:19.

God's grief is echoed when Israel 'grieved Him in the desert,' Psalm 78:40, and 'grieved His Holy Spirit,' Isaiah 63:10, which Paul applies to the church in Ephesians 4:30. God's regret appears again over Saul, 1 Samuel 15:11 and 15:35, in the same chapter that insists He does not change His mind like a man, 1 Samuel 15:29.

In the New Testament, 1 Peter 3:19-20 speaks of spirits who 'disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah,' and 2 Peter 2:4-5 and Jude 6 set angels who sinned beside the ancient world under the flood, texts that many read as allusions to Genesis 6:1-4. Jesus Himself makes 'the days of Noah' the pattern for the days before His return, Matthew 24:37-39 and Luke 17:26-27, stressing not the Nephilim but the ordinariness of a world eating, drinking and marrying until judgment came.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to see why the flood came, and to see that it came from a moral cause. The world did not drown because the gods were irritable or the earth was crowded. It drowned because every boundary God set had been crossed, from the boundary of the one tree in Genesis 3 to the boundary of Abel's life in Genesis 4, and now, in verses 1 to 4, a boundary between heaven and earth or between the godly and the ungodly, depending on how the sons of God are read. In every case the pattern of Genesis 3:6 repeats: seeing, desiring, taking.

He also meant Israel to see the heart of their God. The chapter is remarkable for how much it reveals of what God feels. He does not judge coldly. He is grieved to the heart. Israel, who would themselves grieve God in the wilderness, Psalm 78:40, was meant to understand that sin is not merely the breaking of a rule but the wounding of a relationship.

Finally, he wanted them to hear the word 'But.' Verse 8 is only a few words long, yet it changes everything. Judgment is certain, but it is not the only word. Israel knew what it was to be a people chosen by grace from among the nations, Deuteronomy 7:7-8, and in Noah they were meant to see the first example of that pattern: a man singled out by God's favour in a world under condemnation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is description throughout. It records what the sons of God did, what humanity became, what God felt and what God resolved. None of it is commanded, and the 'mighty men of old, men of renown' are not held up as models. The chapter's silence on their achievements is itself a verdict.

It does carry lasting instruction. The diagnosis of verse 5 remains true of the human heart apart from grace, which is why the New Testament calls for a new heart and new birth rather than moral improvement alone. The grief of God warns believers that their sin matters to Him personally; Paul's command 'do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God,' Ephesians 4:30, makes that explicit. And Jesus applies 'the days of Noah' directly to His hearers, Matthew 24:37-39: ordinary life can carry on, eating and marrying, right up to the moment of judgment, so His people must be ready. The limit of 120 years, on either reading, reminds readers that God's patience has a boundary, which 2 Peter 3:9 turns into an invitation to repent while there is time.

debates.question: Who are the sons of God who took the daughters of men?

views.label: Fallen angelic beings
views.case: Elsewhere in the Old Testament 'sons of God' refers to heavenly beings, Job 1:6, 2:1 and 38:7. The contrast 'sons of God' and 'daughters of men' reads naturally as heaven and earth. The birth of the Nephilim and the severity of the judgment fit an unnatural union. This was the dominant Jewish reading in the period of 1 Enoch and the reading of many early church writers, and 2 Peter 2:4-5 and Jude 6-7, which set angels who sinned beside the flood and speak of 'strange flesh,' are often read as alluding to it. The main objection is Jesus' statement that angels in heaven do not marry, Matthew 22:30.

views.label: The godly line of Seth
views.case: Genesis 4 and 5 contrast Cain's line with Seth's, the line that 'began to call upon the name of the LORD,' Genesis 4:26. On this view the sin is the covenant line marrying without regard to faith, the pattern later forbidden to Israel. It keeps the story on the human plane, where verse 3 and verse 5 place the guilt, and it avoids angels marrying. Augustine held this view, and so did Calvin. Its weakness is that 'sons of God' is never used this way elsewhere in Genesis, and 'daughters of men' in verse 2 seems to mean women generally, the same daughters just born in verse 1.

views.label: Powerful rulers or tyrants
views.case: Ancient kings were often called sons of a god, and the language of taking 'whomever they chose' and producing 'mighty men of renown' fits despots who built harems by force. The word for 'mighty men' is used of Nimrod, the first empire builder, Genesis 10:8. Some Jewish interpreters read the phrase this way. The objection is that no clear biblical example uses 'sons of God' for human kings.

debates.bearing: Serious Christians have held each view, and the passage is famously compressed. What is not in doubt is its function: a boundary was crossed, the pattern of Genesis 3:6 repeated on a larger scale, and the God who set the boundary responded. Verse 3 and verses 5 to 7 place the guilt firmly on humanity, whatever the role of the sons of God.

debates.question: What are the 120 years of verse 3?

views.label: A new limit on the human lifespan
views.case: The phrase 'his days shall be' naturally describes the length of a life, and it follows the long ages of Genesis 5. Moses himself dies at exactly 120, Deuteronomy 34:7. On this reading God shortens human life as a check on growing evil.

views.label: A period of grace before the flood
views.case: Many people after the flood live far longer than 120 years, Shem to 600 and Arphaxad to 438, Genesis 11:10-13, which is hard to square with a fixed lifespan. On this reading the 120 years are a countdown, the time God waits before judgment, which fits 1 Peter 3:20, 'God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built.'

debates.bearing: The countdown reading fits the flood context well, though the lifespan reading has the more natural wording and the gradual decline of ages after the flood in its favour. Either way the verse shows a God who sets a limit to His striving with humanity, and whose patience, though real, is not endless.

debates.question: How can the LORD 'regret' that He made man?

views.label: Real emotion in the language of relationship
views.case: The text does not hedge: the LORD 'regretted' and 'was grieved in His heart.' Scripture repeatedly speaks of God relenting in response to human action, Exodus 32:14, Jeremiah 18:8, Jonah 3:10. On this view God truly responds to His creatures and is not unmoved by their sin.

views.label: Language accommodated to human understanding
views.case: Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say plainly that God is not a man that He should change His mind, and 1 Samuel 15 sets that statement between two notes that the LORD regretted making Saul king, 15:11 and 15:35. The classic Christian answer, found in Augustine and Calvin, is that God's plan does not change but Scripture describes His settled response to evil in terms we can grasp, as a father's sorrow.

debates.bearing: The two views agree more than they differ. God does not discover something He did not know, and His purposes are not frustrated; yet His response to sin is not indifference. The verse is given so that readers feel how much sin matters to God, not so that they doubt His wisdom in creating.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 opens with a phrase, bene ha'elohim, 'sons of God,' whose meaning is the passage's famous puzzle. The construction 'son of' in Hebrew often means 'belonging to the class of,' so that 'sons of the prophets' in 2 Kings 2:3 are members of the prophetic company. The phrase therefore describes a kind of being, and the debate is over which kind. Elsewhere the full phrase is used in Job 1:6, 2:1 and 38:7 of heavenly beings.

The verb in verse 3 translated 'contend,' yadon, is uncertain in meaning. It may be related to din, to judge or strive, which gives the BSB's rendering, but the Septuagint and Syriac read 'remain,' as the footnote notes: 'My Spirit will not remain in man forever.' The reason given, 'for he is mortal,' is literally 'he is flesh,' basar. Flesh in the Old Testament stresses frailty and dependence, 'He is mindful that we are dust,' Psalm 103:14, and the word will recur in the flood account, where the BSB footnote notes that 'all living creatures' is literally 'all flesh,' Genesis 6:12.

The Nephilim of verse 4 are named with a word whose meaning is disputed. Many connect it with naphal, to fall, so either 'fallen ones' or 'those who fall upon' others. The Septuagint translated it 'giants,' and the only other place the word appears is Numbers 13:33, where the spies say 'We even saw the Nephilim there.' The 'mighty men,' gibborim, are warriors; the same word is used of Nimrod, 'a mighty one on the earth,' Genesis 10:8. 'Men of renown' is literally 'men of the name.' The theme of the name runs through these chapters: Seth's line calls 'upon the name of the LORD,' Genesis 4:26, the builders of Babel try to 'make a name for ourselves,' Genesis 11:4, and God promises Abram, 'I will make your name great,' Genesis 12:2. The mighty men had names; the question Genesis presses is who gives a name.

The word for 'inclination' in verse 5, yetser, comes from yatsar, to form or shape, the verb used in Genesis 2:7 when 'the LORD God formed man from the dust.' The shaping of the human heart, what it forms and imagines, has gone wrong. The phrase 'the intent of every thought' in 1 Chronicles 28:9 uses the same pairing, and later Jewish teaching built on this verse its idea of the 'evil inclination' in every person. The verse piles up totality: 'every' inclination, 'altogether' evil, literally 'only evil,' and 'all the time,' literally 'all the day.'

In verse 6 two verbs describe God's response. The first, nacham, 'regretted,' is the verb Lamech used when he named Noah, 'May this one comfort us,' Genesis 5:29. Its range covers both comforting and being moved to change course, and it is the verb used when the LORD 'relented' in Exodus 32:14. The second, 'was grieved,' is from the root atsab, the root behind the 'pain' of childbirth and the 'toil' of the man in Genesis 3:16-17. The pain sin brought into human life is now felt in the heart of God. Notice too the pairing of hearts: the thoughts of man's heart were evil, verse 5, and God was grieved in His heart, verse 6.

The verb 'blot out' in verse 7, machah, means to wipe clean, as 'one wipes out a bowl,' 2 Kings 21:13. It is used again in Genesis 7:4 and 7:23, and later for blotting a name from God's book, Exodus 32:32-33. And 'whom I have created' uses bara, the verb reserved in Genesis 1 for God's creating.

Verse 8 ends on chen, 'favor' or grace, its first appearance in the Bible. The idiom 'find favor in the eyes of' is common later, used of Abraham, Genesis 18:3, and of Moses, Exodus 33:12-13. In Hebrew the name Noah, noach, and chen are written with the same two consonants in reverse order, a wordplay no reader of Hebrew could miss.

typology.type: Noah, the man who found favor in the eyes of the LORD, Genesis 6:8
typology.fulfillment: Noah received favour in a world under judgment, and through him the world was carried through. The correspondence with Christ is real but must be stated with care. Noah found grace as a sinner; Jesus is the Son in whom the Father is 'well pleased,' Luke 3:22, who 'grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man,' Luke 2:52, and who is Himself 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14. Noah received grace; Christ gives it, 'grace upon grace,' John 1:16. Noah saved his household by obeying; Christ saves His people by His own righteousness and death.

typology.type: The days of Noah as a pattern of the last days, Genesis 6:5-7
typology.fulfillment: Jesus uses this generation as the model for the world before His return, Matthew 24:37-39: 'they were oblivious, until the flood came and swept them all away.' The correspondence lies in a world going on with ordinary life while ignoring God, and a judgment that arrives suddenly. The escalation is that the coming of the Son of Man will judge not only the world of one age but all people, and 2 Peter 3:6-7 sets the flood as a preview of the day of judgment. The type falls short because the flood was followed by a promise never to repeat it, Genesis 9:11; the final judgment is final.

typology.type: The grief of God over human sin, Genesis 6:6
typology.fulfillment: God is grieved to the heart over what humanity has become. In the Gospels that grief takes human form. Jesus looks on hardened hearts 'with anger and sorrow,' Mark 3:5, and weeps over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41-42. Isaiah foretold a servant who would be 'a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief,' who 'carried our sorrows,' Isaiah 53:3-4. At the cross grief and judgment meet in one person, as God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. This is a correspondence of theme rather than a formal type, and it shows the flood's grief answered not by another flood but by the Son's own suffering.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through the word grace. Verse 8 is the first time chen appears in Scripture, and it appears against the darkest background yet. That pattern, grace given where sin has grown, is the one Paul states in Romans 5:20: 'where sin increased, grace increased all the more.' The New Testament locates the fullness of that grace in a person. John says the Word 'became flesh,' taking the very frailty that verse 3 names, and that He was 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, and 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,' John 1:17. Noah found favour; in Christ favour comes looking for sinners.

It leads to Christ through the heart of God. Genesis 6:6 is one of the boldest verses in the Old Testament about what God feels. The Gospels show that heart in a human face. Jesus is angered and grieved by hardness of heart, Mark 3:5, He weeps at Lazarus's tomb, John 11:35, and He weeps over the city that will reject Him, Luke 19:41-42. Hebrews says He is a high priest who can 'sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15. The God who grieved in Genesis 6 is not a different God from the Father of Jesus; He is the same God, now made visible.

It leads to Christ through the verdict on the human heart. Verse 5 closes every route of self-rescue. If every inclination of the heart is evil, then the answer cannot be better effort. Paul says that what the law could not do, because it was 'weakened by the flesh,' God did 'by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful man,' Romans 8:3. The flesh that God would not strive with forever in verse 3 is the flesh the Son took on in order to condemn sin in it.

It leads to Christ through Jesus' own reading. When He described the days before His coming, He did not speak about the Nephilim or the sons of God. He spoke of people 'eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage,' Matthew 24:38. The danger He drew from Genesis 6 was not exotic evil but ordinary indifference, a world too busy to notice that judgment was near.

A caution belongs here. The passage is not a hidden picture of the incarnation in its account of the sons of God, and reading verses 1 to 4 as a prophecy of Christ goes beyond the text. The link to Christ runs through the themes the passage plainly sets out: the ruin of the human heart, the grief of God, the certainty of judgment and the surprising favour that rests on one man. Each is fulfilled in Jesus, who bears the judgment, reveals the grief and brings the grace.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the One who sees. Three times Genesis 6 uses the verb. The sons of God saw the daughters of men, verse 2; the LORD saw the wickedness of man, verse 5; and Noah found favour in the eyes of the LORD, verse 8. Human seeing leads to taking. God's seeing is complete, reaching past actions to 'every inclination of the thoughts of his heart.' The same God who 'searches every heart,' 1 Chronicles 28:9, is not deceived by what the mighty men of renown achieved.

It shows God as the One whose Spirit sustains human life and who may withdraw it. Verse 3 speaks of 'My Spirit' in relation to humanity, which recalls Genesis 1:2 and the breath of life given in Genesis 2:7. Life in the flesh is held up by God's Spirit, and when God sets a limit, He is not merely punishing but ceasing to hold back what sin deserves.

It shows God as a Person who feels. The language of verse 6 is emotional, and the Bible does not apologise for it. God is not the unmoved force of philosophy, untouched by the world. Yet the passage does not make God fickle. Numbers 23:19 insists that God 'is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind.' The Christian tradition has held both truths together: God's purposes are unchanging, and His response to sin is real sorrow. What changes in Genesis 6 is not God's character but His dealings with a world that has changed. His holiness and His love both stay constant, and it is precisely because both are constant that He grieves.

It shows God as Judge whose justice is measured. Before judgment falls He sets a limit of 120 years, verse 3, and 1 Peter 3:20 describes that period as God waiting 'patiently.' Judgment comes, but it comes late, after long patience, and it comes from a heart that finds no pleasure in it. Ezekiel 18:23 asks, 'Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?' and Hosea 11:8 shows God's heart turning within Him at the thought of destroying His people.

Above all it shows God as the One who gives grace freely. The text says nothing about Noah deserving favour before it tells us he found it. The description of his righteousness comes only in verse 9. Grace is the first thing said about Noah, and the order is part of the message. God's favour is not a wage but a gift, 'justified freely by His grace,' Romans 3:24.

For worship, the passage asks for sobriety and gratitude. Sobriety, because God sees every heart and grieves over sin. Gratitude, because the God who has every reason to wipe the world clean chooses to begin again with one man, and in that choice keeps His promise to the woman's seed.

crossReferences.note: The woman saw that the tree was good and took. The sons of God saw that the daughters of men were good, the BSB's 'beautiful,' and took, Genesis 6:2. The same three verbs show that the sin of the garden has been reproduced on a larger scale, desire leading to seizure.

One of the Old Testament's clearest uses of 'sons of God' for heavenly beings who present themselves before the LORD, with Satan among them. It is the main textual support for the angelic reading of Genesis 6:2, and it shows that the phrase could name members of God's heavenly court.

The only other appearance of the Nephilim. The spies report giants in Canaan, 'the descendants of Anak that come from the Nephilim,' and feel like grasshoppers. Genesis 6:4's note that the Nephilim were there 'afterward as well' may prepare for this, and it reminds Israel that God has dealt with giants before.

After the flood God repeats the diagnosis of Genesis 6:5, 'every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth,' but draws the opposite conclusion: never again will He curse the ground or destroy all living creatures. The flood has not changed the human heart; God's covenant patience must carry the world from here.

Samuel says God 'does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man,' in a chapter that twice says the LORD regretted making Saul king, 15:11 and 15:35. Read with Genesis 6:6, it guards against thinking God is fickle while keeping the reality of His sorrow over sin.

Paul warns believers, 'do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.' The idea that human sin grieves God goes back to Genesis 6:6 and runs through Isaiah 63:10. Paul adds that believers are sealed for redemption, so their sin grieves One who has already bound Himself to them.

Jesus reaches back to this generation to describe the world before His return. People went on eating, drinking and marrying, oblivious until the flood swept them away. He takes from Genesis 6 not the exotic features of the Nephilim but the ordinary indifference of a world ripe for judgment.

Peter speaks of spirits who disobeyed 'when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built.' The phrase interprets the 120 years of Genesis 6:3 as a time of patient waiting, and many readers connect these spirits with the sons of God of Genesis 6:2.

Peter sets two examples side by side: God did not spare the angels when they sinned, and He did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah. The pairing suggests Peter read the rebellion of Genesis 6:1-4 and the flood together, and it makes Noah's rescue a pledge that God knows how to rescue the godly.

'The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure.' Jeremiah restates Genesis 6:5 for Israel on the eve of exile. The same diagnosis that led to the flood leads to Babylon, and it is why Jeremiah 31 promises a new covenant with the law written on the heart.

'Where sin increased, grace increased all the more.' Genesis 6 is the first great example. Sin has multiplied until every inclination is evil, and at that point the Bible's first mention of grace appears, resting on Noah. Paul sees the same pattern reach its height in Christ.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as He approaches it, knowing its coming judgment. The grief of God at human sin in Genesis 6:6 appears here on a human face. Judgment is still coming, but it is announced with tears, not with indifference.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 6:1-8 is where the story of the fall reaches its first full measure. Genesis 3 showed sin entering through one act of seeing and taking. Genesis 4 showed it spreading to murder and to Lamech's boast of vengeance. Genesis 5 showed death reigning through the generations. Now it has filled the earth, and the narrator can say that every inclination of the human heart is only evil all the time. The question the fall raised, what will God do with a world that has turned against Him, is here answered in two words at once: judgment and grace.

Judgment, because a holy God cannot leave a world like this as it is. The un-making of creation announced in verse 7 prepares the flood of chapters 7 and 8, where the waters of Genesis 1:2 return. Grace, because the same verse that announces the end is followed by 'But Noah.' God does not abandon His plan for creation or His promise of the woman's seed. He narrows it to one man and carries it through.

The pattern set here recurs throughout the story of redemption. Again and again sin comes to its full measure, and God judges while preserving a remnant by grace. Sodom falls while Lot is rescued; Israel goes into exile while a remnant returns. The prophets speak of a remnant chosen by grace, and Paul applies the same phrase to his own day, Romans 11:5. Each time the question is whether sin will finally win, and each time God preserves a line through which His promise continues.

The pattern comes to its climax in Christ. The grief of God over sin is taken into the heart of the Son, who weeps over the city that will crucify Him. The judgment God pronounced on all flesh falls on the Son who became flesh. And the favour that rested on Noah rests fully on Jesus, the beloved Son in whom the Father is well pleased, so that all who are in Him share it. 'The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone,' Titus 2:11.

The new creation is where this passage finally resolves. The heart whose every inclination was evil will be replaced; God promises a new heart and a new spirit, Ezekiel 36:26. The grief of God over what humanity has become will give way to His joy over a people made new. The flood un-made a corrupt world once; the day of the Lord will bring a new heavens and a new earth 'where righteousness dwells,' 2 Peter 3:13. And the favour first found by one man will be the settled condition of a whole redeemed humanity.

quiz.q: How does the passage describe the state of the human heart before the flood?

options.text: Every inclination of the thoughts of the heart was only evil all the time.
options.note: Sin had become the settled bent of the whole human heart.

options.text: The heart was a mix of good and evil in equal measure.
options.note: The text is starker; it says the inclination was only evil continually.

options.text: The heart was basically good but occasionally tempted.
options.note: This softens the passage, which describes wickedness as great and constant.

options.text: The heart had become perfectly pure again.
options.note: The opposite; the wickedness of man was great upon the earth.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the LORD regretted making man and was grieved in His heart?

options.text: God feels the offense of sin deeply, sorrowing over evil without changing His character or being mistaken.
options.note: The words reveal a God genuinely grieved by sin, not a God who erred.

options.text: God admitted He had made a mistake He could not foresee.
options.note: The language shows real sorrow, but Scripture does not present God as caught off guard or wrong.

options.text: God felt nothing and acted purely mechanically.
options.note: The text stresses the opposite; He was grieved in His heart.

options.text: God decided humanity was never worth making at all.
options.note: His grief coexists with grace, and He preserves Noah and the promise.

quiz.q: What is significant about the word used for Noah finding favor?

options.text: It is the first appearance of grace in the Bible, and it rests on Noah before he is called righteous.
options.note: Grace comes first, foreshadowing the gospel pattern.

options.text: It means Noah earned God's approval by his hard work.
options.note: The word is grace, unmerited favor, not earned reward, though Noah is later called righteous.

options.text: It simply means Noah was lucky.
options.note: It is not luck but God's gracious favor resting on Noah.

options.text: It means God favored Noah's whole city.
options.note: The favor rests on Noah, the one exception in a corrupt world.

quiz.q: How does Noah point forward to Christ in this passage?

options.text: As the one who finds grace and through whom the world is spared, he prefigures the righteous One who saves a people from judgment.
options.note: 1 Peter 3 reads Noah's rescue as a pattern of salvation in Christ.

options.text: Because Noah personally forgave everyone's sins.
options.note: Noah does not forgive sins; he foreshadows Christ as the favored, righteous rescuer.

options.text: Because Noah preached to angels.
options.note: That is not the point here; Noah pictures the one through whom God saves.

options.text: Noah has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The New Testament repeatedly links Noah's rescue to salvation in Christ.

quiz.q: Why is the identity of the sons of God best held with humility?

options.text: Serious interpreters differ among the angelic, Sethite, and ruler views, yet the passage's point is unchanged.
options.note: The main message stands whichever view is correct.

options.text: Because the Bible clearly names them and no debate exists.
options.note: The text is actually terse, and faithful readers have long disagreed.

options.text: Because the answer changes the entire meaning of salvation.
options.note: The gospel does not hinge on this detail; the point is corruption and coming judgment.

options.text: Because it proves the passage is only a myth.
options.note: Difficulty of a detail does not make the account untrue; it presents real history.

questions: The passage says sin had become the constant bent of the human heart. When you are honest, where do you notice your own heart leaning away from God by default rather than by rare accident?
God was genuinely grieved by human evil. How does it change your view of sin to realize it is not merely breaking rules but wounding the heart of the God who made you?
In a world gone wrong, grace came to rest on one man before anything is said about his goodness. Where do you need to hear that God's grace comes to you first, not as a reward you must earn?
Jesus said the days of Noah picture the world's readiness for His return. How awake or asleep is your heart to the reality that God will one day set everything right?
The whole world was corrupt, yet Noah walked differently. Where is God calling you to stand apart from the current of the crowd around you this week?

translationNotes.note: My Spirit will not contend with man forever can also be rendered My Spirit will not remain in man forever; the 120 years is read either as a new limit on the human lifespan or as a countdown of patience before the flood.

The LORD regretted, or was sorry, translates a word that elsewhere means to relent or be comforted; it expresses genuine divine grief over sin, not a confession that God made an error, since Scripture affirms He knows all things.
